content: It is determined by calculating the average sequence distance between residues that form native contacts in the folded protein, normalized by the total length of the protein. Proteins with higher contact orders tend to exhibit longer folding times, whereas proteins with lower contact orders are associated with faster folding. Low contact order has also been proposed as an indicator of potential downhill folding, a process in which protein folding occurs without a significant free energy barrier. This phenomenon is thought to arise from the reduced loss of conformational entropy when local contacts are formed, as opposed to nonlocal contacts. Protein structure prediction methods are generally more accurate when applied to proteins with low contact orders. This increased accuracy may partly be due to the smaller size of low-contact-order proteins, but it is more likely explained by the reduced number of possible long-range residue-residue interactions that need to be considered during global optimization processes aimed at minimizing an energy function. Even advanced structure prediction methods, such as the Rosetta method, tend to overproduce structural predictions with low contact orders compared to the distributions observed in experimentally determined protein structures. The percentage of native contact order in a protein can also serve as a metric for assessing the nativeness of folding transition states. Psi value analysis, when combined with molecular dynamics simulations, has been used to generate transition-state models. These models often exhibit contact orders that closely resemble those of the fully folded state, particularly in small, fast-folding proteins. Furthermore, the contact orders observed in both transition states and native states are strongly correlated with the overall folding time of the protein. In addition to their utility in structure prediction, contact orders can themselves be predicted based on sequence alignments. This capability can be valuable for classifying the fold of a novel protein sequence, especially when the sequence shares some degree of homology with known protein sequences.
